# Diagnosing a Single-Beam Failure in an H4 Headlight System

When a driver's side low beam fails while daytime running lights (DRL) and high beams function correctly on that same side, the issue is almost certainly isolated to the low-beam filament or its specific control circuit. In many vehicles manufactured around 2009, including the Honda CR-V, the headlight assembly often utilizes an H4 bulb. This single glass envelope houses two distinct filaments within one base: one dedicated to high-intensity lighting (high beam) and another for low-intensity driving (low beam).

The fact that your DRL and high beams are working confirms that the power supply reaching the socket, the main ground connection, and the bulb's base integrity are sound. It effectively rules out a blown fuse affecting the entire headlight cluster, as you have already verified the fuse under the steering column. Furthermore, since the passenger side is fully operational, the issue is not a shared relay failure or a broken wiring harness running from the engine bay to the bumper.

### Filament Independence and Bulb Replacement

The core technical principle here is filament independence. Inside an H4 bulb, the high-beam filament and the low-beam filament are electrically separate components sharing a common ground path but distinct power inputs. When the low beam fails but the other two modes work, the high-beam filament has likely not burned out yet, or it is operating in a different circuit configuration depending on the car's lighting logic.

The most direct solution is replacing the bulb. Since the H4 design separates these functions physically within one unit, you cannot replace just the low-beam filament; you must swap the entire bulb. This is a standard trade-off in automotive engineering that simplifies assembly but increases cost if one function fails. When purchasing a replacement for a 2009 Honda CR-V, ensure you select an Sylvania or equivalent OEM-grade H4 bulb. Cheap aftermarket variants sometimes have inconsistent filament placement or sub-par glass quality, which can lead to premature failure of the remaining functional filament after installation.

### The Daytime Running Light Circuit Logic

It is also worth noting how the vehicle's lighting control module (LCM) interacts with these filaments. In modern Honda architectures, the DRL often bypasses the standard headlight switch and runs directly from a constant battery feed to the high-beam filament of the H4 bulb. This explains why your DRL works while the low beam is dead; the system is successfully energizing one filament but failing to energize the other.

If you were to inspect the wiring harness behind the headlight housing, you would typically find three or four wires connecting to the base: one for ground (shared), one for the high-beam feed, and one for the low-beam feed. A visual inspection might reveal a corroded pin in the socket specifically corresponding to the low-beam terminal. Corrosion here can create enough resistance to prevent the filament from glowing, even if the fuse is intact. Cleaning the contacts with electrical contact cleaner before installing a new bulb is a recommended step, as oxidation is a common culprit for partial failures in older vehicles exposed to road salt and moisture.

### Relays and Switches

While less likely given that the high beam works on the same side, it is prudent to check the headlight relay if the issue persists after bulb replacement. The low beam and high beam often share a single relay in some configurations, or they may be controlled by separate relays depending on the specific trim level of the CR-V. If replacing the bulb and cleaning the socket yields no results, the next diagnostic step involves swapping the known-good headlight relay from one side to the other. If the failure follows the relay, the issue lies in the switching mechanism rather than the bulb itself.

Ultimately, for a 2009 model, component wear is expected. The H4 bulb is designed with both filaments in mind, and when one reaches the end of its lifespan, it does so independently. Replacing the bulb resolves the electrical continuity issue, restoring full functionality to the headlight assembly.
